extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and exercises from a journalism/textbook chapter on writing vivid figurative language and on how to read and write book reviews (especially aimed at high‑school students). Covers criteria for fiction, non‑fiction and collections and practice exercises for similes/metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the book thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: The first bit of advice on reviewing, then, is to read the book thoughtfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful reading is the best preparation for reviewing. If you have read a book superficially, missed the point of the story, or failed to grasp its strength or weakness, your review will be correspondingly superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience — review for readers, not author/publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewer must remember that he is reviewing the book for the benefit of his readers and not for the author or publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High‑school reviewers should aim their remarks at peers ('Tell me a book to get from the library' or 'Is it any good?') rather than attempting to please the author or publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give your own reaction and be sincere
rubrics_metrics.description: The student's book review should give his own reaction to the book... Unless sincerity characterizes his estimate, his review is valueless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express personal response; if you dislike the book, say so and back your opinion with specific references to the work. Avoid adopting opinions you don't genuinely hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid restating jacket blurbs or grown-up opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: What it should not be is a reiteration of what some grown-up thinks, or a high‑sounding report that the student believes is expected of him, nor yet a rehash of what the jacket says.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce original judgment and evidence rather than repeating publicity copy or others' critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague generalities
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no rule or formula for the writing of a book review. The taste of the reviewer and his ingenuity must combine to set forth his reaction with charm and sincerity. Vague generalities are taboo as in all other good writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims with specific references and examples from the book; be concrete rather than general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer three core questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Here are three questions that he should answer in judging a book: What did the author set out to do? Did he do it? How well did he do it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as organizing criteria for the review: identify the author's purpose, judge its fulfillment, and evaluate the quality of execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and learn the classics to ground judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: To become a good reviewer the student should read the best in literature, the classics, that have stood the test of time. Otherwise, he will have no real basis for his judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden reading to develop standards and comparative perspective for evaluating new works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction review: identify type, manner, and comment on plot/character
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell what type the book is ... and give the author. Hint at his manner of telling the story. Then comment specifically on the hero or heroine ... or the situation that motivates the story or the plot ... Set the stage and then etch a few details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not give the solution away or reveal the surprise if it is that kind of story. Don't tell the story. Draw conclusions as to general interest, noting reality to life or its lack, specific weaknesses, and whether it was satisfying or disappointing; compare with other works by the same author if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑fiction review: state scope and provide specific references
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑fiction will be handled in the light of your historical, scientific, or literary taste and background, but you will want to judge by answering substantially the same questions ... The reader will want to know the scope of the work and your reaction, with references specific enough to make him experience parts of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell readers what the book covers, how well it accomplishes that purpose, and give concrete examples or passages to illustrate strengths or weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing collections: build a general impression and cite examples
rubrics_metrics.description: As you read through poem after poem, play after play, you build up a general idea of the character of the book. When you finish you recall those that you enjoyed most. ... The reader will want to know the names of several of the poems or plays, and extracts sufficient to show what you liked—or what you thought made the collection milk and water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested plan for collections: 1) Give scope of the collection; author. 2) Make a general comment on quality, tone, interest. 3) Suggest some of the titles. What do they reveal? 4) Mention the most appealing poem/play/essay and why. 5) Make specific comment on individual items and quote to support points. 6) End with a terse clinching comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek first the aim of the book; then judge
rubrics_metrics.description: CAUTION: Seek first the aim of the book; then judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the author's stated or implied purpose before evaluating success; avoid judging by irrelevant standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style expectations for reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of words, vivid imagery and grace of style should characterize all book reviews. 'Transitions should be carefully made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise diction, vivid examples, smooth transitions and an engaging tone appropriate to the readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simile and metaphor to clarify and supply deficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists, like poets, use the simile and the metaphor to clarify a thing not well known through a thing that is well known, and to supply deficiencies in the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare unfamiliar objects/ideas to familiar ones to make images vivid; exercises follow to practice this device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make similes feel true — 'you must feel the likeness'
rubrics_metrics.description: You must feel the likeness if you would make a striking image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only make comparisons that honestly convey a perceived similarity; forced or fanciful comparisons that don't 'feel' right will not be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensify images by omitting 'like' or 'as' (use metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: In all the comparisons above you have expressed the comparison by use of a word such as like or as. Omit it and you will intensify each image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: 'The moon is like an orange balloon.' vs. metaphoric form used by poets (e.g., 'The moon is a ghostly galleon'). Using direct metaphor often produces a stronger image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use action (verbs) to imply comparisons — metaphor by verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Take any common thing—moonlight, for example. Think of a thing that it resembles to your imagination, but do not tell what the thing is. Make the first thing do something that is a characteristic action of the second. EXAMPLE: The moonlight withers from the sky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the subject perform an action characteristic of the implicit comparison to create a vivid, compact metaphor (verb-driven imagery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice creating original images and exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises asking students to compare common things to familiar things, to omit like/as, to use verbs for implied comparisons, and to invent striking images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete assigned exercises (lists of prompts are provided) to build the habit of seeing likenesses and producing vivid figurative language; examples and model metaphors are given as guidance.
